column2: Khosravani investing system, Fundamental Investing System, fundamental investing system
Dr Bardia Khosravani’s Fundamental Investing System: fundamental analysis with Codal, focused on dividend-focused stocks, for passive income and financial freedom.
Managing your mind and your financial life
The other side of the coin: managing fear and greed, biases, position size, and fitting your investing to your financial life.
Emergency money
6 to 12 months of living costs, outside stocks, in a fixed-income fund or short-term deposit, so a market fall doesn’t force you to sell.
Bucketing
Current costs in a bank account, the emergency fund, 1 to 3-year goals in fixed income, Akhza or gold, and growth capital (5 years and up) in stocks.
Statement

One page of rules you sign with yourself: a real-return target, the maximum fall you can bear, a cap per stock and per industry, selling conditions, and things you never do (leverage, signals, borrowed money).
Paper portfolio
Hypothetical portfolio
A hypothetical portfolio with a written reason for each purchase, kept for at least 3 months before real money, with its result compared against the overall index and a fixed-income fund.
Journal
Recording every decision with its reason, forecast and date, before acting. Forecast errors are the best teacher.
codal, Codal system

The Comprehensive System for Publishers’ Information (codal.ir): the official home of monthly reports, financial statements, announcements and meeting minutes of companies on the Tehran Stock Exchange and Farabourse.
Exchange technology management website
The trading-data website: price, volume, share count, major shareholders, and retail and institutional buying and selling.
Exchange organization
SEO, Securities and Exchange Organization
The capital market regulator: disclosure rules, capital-increase permits and market rules.
Farabourse and the base market
base market, yellow, orange, red
Farabourse has a first market, a second market and a base market. The base market means the company doesn’t meet all the conditions; weaker disclosure and more risk.
Where prices are discovered for goods such as steel, petrochemicals, cement and copper; it shows next month’s selling price earlier than Codal.
Sejam
Share ownership registration, Sejam and dividend payment; it shows when a dividend actually arrives.
Nominal return
The percent change in money, ignoring inflation.
Real return
The change in purchasing power: (1 + nominal return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1. A 40% return with 45% inflation means you’ve become poorer.
Islamic treasury bills
Government bonds whose yield to maturity is the benchmark for the nominal risk-free rate.
The return you get without stock risk, such as the yield to maturity of Akhza or a fixed-income fund. If a stock doesn’t pay more, you’ve taken the risk for nothing.
Risk premium
Risk premium, premium
The extra return you demand for taking stock risk; usually 5 to 10 percentage points above the risk-free rate.
A company’s ability to raise its selling prices in step with inflation or the exchange rate. The most important first filter of FIS in Iran.
Fundamental analysis
Fundamentals
It asks how much money the company makes and what it’s worth; its data is Codal, commodity prices and exchange rates. FIS is fundamental.
Technical analysis
It asks which way the price will go; its data is price and volume charts. In Iran’s market, with daily price limits and queues, it is very noisy.
Daily price limit
buy queue, sell queue
The cap on the daily price change. When it’s hit, a queue forms and you may not be able to sell for several days.
Retail and institutional
retail money, smart money
Retail means individuals and institutional means organisations. Retail money coming in and “smart money” are trading-board data, and in FIS they are only for timing, not a reason to buy.
Market cap
The whole company’s price: price × total number of shares.
Shows a period’s sales, costs and profit: from operating income to net profit.
Statement of financial position
Assets, liabilities and equity on a given date.
Statement of cash flows
The real cash that came in or went out through operations, investing and financing.
Equity
Shareholders’ equity
Shareholders’ share of the assets: capital, reserves and accumulated profit. In Iran it is at historical cost.
The money that comes from the company’s main business, that is, selling goods or services.
The cost of making or buying the goods sold: materials, wages and overheads.
Gross profit margin
Gross profit ÷ sales. A thin margin means high sensitivity to the product price and costs.
Profit from the company’s main business after selling and admin costs. The most repeatable part of profit.
Profit after finance costs, non-operating items and tax. It may contain one-off items.
Earnings per share
Net profit ÷ number of shares. For valuation, sustainable EPS (without one-off items) is what matters.
Dividend per share
The dividend per share approved by the general meeting.
Auditor’s report
Auditor’s opinion
Four types: unqualified (no material problem), qualified (a material but limited problem), adverse (the statements are misleading), and disclaimer (there wasn’t enough evidence).
Qualification paragraph
The part of the auditor’s report that explains a problem. What matters is the amount and nature of the paragraph, not merely that it exists.
Separate and consolidated
Consolidated statements
Separate is only the parent company; consolidated is the whole group as one company. Consolidated being far below separate year after year means the group is weaker than it looks.
Interim statements
6-month, 3-month, 9-month
Quarterly and 6-month reports, usually unaudited or only reviewed; compare them with the same-length period of the previous year.
The quantity, price and value of each month’s sales and production. The earliest official number on the sales trend.
Volume and price
volume growth, price growth
Sales value = volume × price. Value growing while volume falls is a warning.
Material information
An announcement of an event that may change the price or an investor’s decision, such as an accident, a big contract or a price change.
Management report
Management’s explanation of performance, plans and outlook; check its numbers against the statements.
General meeting
Held no later than 4 months after the end of the financial year, and approves the DPS.
A meeting for basic decisions such as a capital increase, a change to the articles of association, or Article 141.
From cash contributions (new money), accumulated profit, revaluation or share premium. Only contributions and share premium bring new money.
The right to buy a new share at the nominal value of 1,000 rials in a capital increase from contributions. Theoretical value ≈ share price − 1,000.
Adjusted price
The price after a capital increase: (P + 1,000 × a) ÷ (1 + a + b); a is the contribution share and b the accumulated-profit share.
Payout
DPS ÷ EPS: what part of profit is paid out in cash. The Commercial Code requires at least 10%.
Previous years’ undistributed profits that have stayed in equity.
Notes to the statements
Note
The detail behind each number in the financial statements: sales broken down, cost of sales, receivables, other income, tax and commitments.
Brackets in financial statements
Negative number
A number in brackets is negative; for example a cost that is subtracted from profit.
Receivables
Credit sales whose money hasn’t arrived yet. If they grow much faster than sales, profit quality goes down.
Goods and materials in the warehouse. A build-up is a prelude to write-downs or falling demand.
Income from outside the main business, such as gains on selling assets, deposit interest or currency translation. Usually removed from sustainable profit.
Translation
Gains or losses from a change in the exchange rate on foreign-currency assets or debts. Removed from sustainable profit; check exporters separately.
Group companies or the major shareholder. Selling to them below market, or not collecting their receivables, is a red flag.
Removing one-off items such as asset sales, translation gains and provision reversals, so that what is left is profit that will repeat next year too.
Sustainable profit
Sustainable EPS
Profit that will repeat next year too: normal volume × current price − real costs.
Price-to-earnings ratio
Price ÷ EPS. Work it out with sustainable profit; a low P/E on its own doesn’t mean cheap.
EPS ÷ price; the inverse of P/E. In Iran it should be compared with the Akhza yield plus a risk premium.
Expected return
Roughly E/P × payout ratio + profit growth. It must beat Akhza + the risk premium.
Payback
payback, payback period
How many years it takes for growing EPS to add up to today’s price. FIS rule of thumb: under about 4 to 5 years.
Profit quality
Operating cash ÷ net profit. Above 0.8 is good; below 0.5 needs a close look.
Replacement value
The cost of rebuilding the assets at today’s prices. A price below it, with no profit, isn’t cheapness.
upstream, downstream
Upstream, midstream and downstream. One link’s selling price is the next link’s cost of sales.
Operating leverage
How much profit moves with a change in the product price, the exchange rate or feedstock. A thin margin means high sensitivity.
Dilution
A fall in each shareholder’s stake and return, for example when capital-increase money is spent at a return below the current E/P.
Selection funnel
Five stages: first screening, business, balance sheet, price and value trigger.
Portfolio rules
Starting point: 8 to 15 companies, at most 10 to 15% per stock and 25 to 30% per industry.
A sign that calls for a close look, such as growing sales value with falling volume, or repeated capital increases.
The three FIS conditions: sustainable profit-making, a high payout, and profit growth above inflation.
capital-focused stock, growth-focused
Pays out a big part of its profit in cash every year, and the return comes more from DPS; as opposed to a capital-focused stock that keeps profit for growth.
DPS ÷ price. A price of 5,000 and a DPS of 1,000 means a 20% dividend yield.
Theoretical price after the meeting
Price adjustment after the meeting
On the reopening day after the meeting, theoretical price = previous price − DPS. Wealth doesn’t change.
Free asset
When the total dividends received equal the money paid to buy; the original capital has come back and the stock is effectively free (in accounting terms, under inflation).
Required capital = monthly costs × 12 ÷ dividend yield. DPS must grow at least as fast as inflation.
Analysis profile
A short FIS-style analysis: industry and product, what sets the prices, major shareholder, return record, P/E, assumptions, sensitivity, and the sentence “This is analysis, not a buy recommendation.”
Discounted cash flow
Valuation by discounting future free cash flow; for a company whose profit today doesn’t represent its future.
Free cash flow
The cash left for shareholders and lenders after operating costs, tax and the necessary investment.
Discount rate
The required return for discounting cash flow. In Iran, by the build-up method: Akhza + equity risk premium + company-specific risk premium.
Weighted average cost of capital
Equity weight × cost of equity + debt weight × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate).
Terminal value
TV, terminal
The value of all years after the forecast period: next year’s flow ÷ (discount rate − terminal growth). Usually 70 to 85% of total value.
Nominal and real
Consistency
Nominal cash flow is discounted at a nominal rate, and real at a real rate. Mixing them is the most common error.
Enterprise value
Market value of equity + bank debt − free cash − non-operating investments + non-controlling interests.
Operating profit + depreciation. Used in the EV/EBITDA multiple.
Market value to assets ratio
Market value ÷ total assets. One of the columns of Dr Khosravani’s analysis template on his Telegram channel.
Margin with conservative profit
FIS profit ÷ operating income. In his posts it is usually lower than “operating profit ÷ sales”, because FIS profit leaves out non-repeating items.
Market value to 80% of net asset value
His measure for holdings: market value ÷ (0.8 × NAV). Below 100% means the market prices the holding below 80% of its assets.
Price-to-book ratio
Price ÷ book value per share. Of little meaning in Iran because assets are at historical cost.
Three-statement model
Excel model
Future income statement, balance sheet and cash flow, linked together, with the value coming out of that same forecast.
Accruals
(Net profit − operating cash) ÷ average total assets. High means a big part of profit hasn’t turned into cash.
Return on invested capital
NOPAT ÷ capital employed. In Iran the denominator is historical, so nominal ROIC is higher than the real figure.
Operating profit after tax; the numerator of ROIC.
Capital employed
Net fixed assets + trade receivables + inventory − trade payables.
Competitive advantage
Moat
What protects a company’s profit from competitors: cost, brand, a scarce licence, customer switching costs, or a policy advantage (which isn’t permanent).
Inventory profit
Hidden inflation
Under inflation, goods made more cheaply are sold at today’s price and the margin looks better than it really is.
Earnings management
Manipulating the timing or size of profit; signs: profit without cash, a change in depreciation method, provision reversals, late publication and a sudden change of auditor.
Buying or selling because others do: sitting in queues and Telegram signals. Antidote: only with a Codal file and numbers.
Clinging to an irrelevant number such as a previous high or your buying price. Antidote: compare the price with today’s value.
Selling the profitable stock and holding the losing one until it “gets back to the buying price”. Antidote: “If I didn’t own it today, would I buy it?”
Confirmation bias
Only reading news that agrees with you. Antidote: write the best opposing argument.
After a rising market everyone thinks they’re an analyst. Antidote: record your forecasts and score them.
The chance of a loss so big you can’t carry on. Its sources in Iran: leverage, concentration and the wrong money.
Leverage
Broker credit
Buying with money borrowed from the broker or a loan. With daily price limits and sell queues, a forced sale can happen; FIS doesn’t use leverage.
Position size
What share of the portfolio is in one stock. With a 10% cap, even a 60% fall in one stock is only 6% of the whole portfolio.
Seven update steps
7 steps
For each report: classify, compare with your forecast, rial effect, permanent or temporary, update the model, compare with the portfolio rules, write in the notebook.
Whether the company reports on time, fully and clearly. Delays and unexplained corrections call for a higher risk premium.
Net asset value
For a holding: (market value of listed shares + estimated value of unlisted holdings + other assets − liabilities − tax on a hypothetical sale) ÷ number of shares.
Non-controlling interests
Minority interest
Other shareholders’ share of subsidiaries in the consolidated statements.
Article 141
Accumulated losses
When accumulated losses exceed half the capital, an extraordinary meeting must decide on dissolving or continuing.
Revaluation
Updating the book value of assets; a capital increase from it brings no new money and is sometimes a way to escape Article 141.
option, call option, put option
A contract for the right to buy or sell at a set price. Not a main tool in FIS; a put only as temporary insurance.
Embedded put option
Embedded guarantee
A set loss floor for the shareholder; but also look at the risk of the guaranteeing issuer.
FIS score
scoring system, FIS rank, 11 variables

Khosravani and Ajorlou’s 1405 paper: the sum of step scores for 11 variables, from 0 to 100. Forward P/E and cumulative sales growth are 15 each; profit margin, margin trend growth, forward P/S, payout ratio and receivables-to-assets ratio 10 each; earnings expectation gap, collection period, inventory turnover period and financial year 5 each.
Return on equity
ROE, return on shareholders’ capital
Net profit ÷ equity; how much profit each toman of shareholders’ capital has made. A rising trend is a good sign.
receivables, amounts receivable

Receivables ÷ total sales × days in the period: how many days it takes for credit sales to turn into cash. Below the company’s own average means sales turn into money sooner. One of the 11 FIS variables.
inventory turnover, warehouse
Average inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × days in the period: how many days it takes for goods to turn into money. Above the company’s own average means sales have slowed. One of the 11 FIS variables.
Operating cash to current liabilities ratio
operating cash flow, ability to pay debts
Net cash from operations ÷ current liabilities; the ability to pay short-term debts from operating money.
Initial public offering
IPO, new share offering
A company’s first offering of shares on the exchange. In FIS it’s weighed like any other stock: the offer price against value and the profit forecast.
P/E Forward, leading P/E
Price ÷ forecast earnings per share to the end of the financial year. In the FIS paper, forecast profit = average monthly profit of the past months × 12. The highest-scoring FIS variable (15 points).
Trailing P/E
P/E TTM, historical P/E
Price ÷ earnings per share for the past 12 months.
P/S Forward, price to sales
Market value ÷ forecast sales to the end of the financial year. One of the 11 FIS variables.
Forward and trailing P/E
|forward P/E − trailing P/E| ÷ trailing P/E × 100; shows whether the market expects future profit to grow or fall. One of the 11 FIS variables.
Revenue growth
Sales in the current period against the same period last year, in percent. One of the two 15-point FIS variables.
FIS profit
Conservative profit
In the FIS paper: profit without non-operating or non-repeating income and items; the basis of the profit margin.
receivables, credit sales
Total receivables ÷ total assets × 100; how much the company relies on credit sales. One of the 11 FIS variables.
threshold, partial score
Several thresholds for each variable; each band has a fixed score, and no more points come until the next threshold is passed. The FIS scoring method.
MAE and MFE
maximum adverse excursion, maximum favourable excursion
The biggest fall and biggest rise in price relative to the buying price during the holding period. In the FIS paper’s portfolio the averages were about 30% and 316%.
Coefficient of determination
R², regression
The share of the differences in one variable (e.g. return) that is explained by another variable (e.g. score); between 0 and 1. About 0.75 in the FIS paper.
price to dividend, forward P/D
Market value ÷ forecast dividend (forecast net profit × payout ratio): how many years of dividends until the purchase money comes back. In Dr Khosravani’s videos, about 3 is ideal.
FIS indicator
buy at 4, sell at 8
In Dr Khosravani’s videos: buy price = the average of the prices that make forward P/E and P/D equal 4; sell price = the same with 8.
stop-loss, exit
Selling because the company becomes loss-making, its profit margin falls or its quarterly sales fall, not because of a percentage price fall.
Priced in
High P/E
In Dr Khosravani’s videos: a stock with a forward P/E of 8 to 12 that already has future growth in its price and carries a risk of a big fall.
Comparing with gold
Dr Khosravani’s benchmark for every asset: the return must beat gold; an asset lagging gold gets turned into gold.
The Bir rule
keeping one share
Dr Khosravani’s personal rule in the videos: when selling a stock, he keeps one share of it.
